title: Measuring Scribal Literacy Through Quantitative Analysis
text:
Protosnap’s Methods


1 2 3 4 5





Stable Diffusion model trained specifically on cuneiform images for deep image understanding (SD)
This allows recognition of wedge impressions even with varying lighting, damage, and material textures
Deep diffusion features are used to find matches between prototype images (cuneiform fonts) and sign samples (“best buddy correspondences”)
Two-step alignment

Global alignment: roughly positions the prototype over the photo
Local refinement: adjusts each wedge to its precise location on the tablet

Match each prototype wedge to its impression in the tablet photo

title: Measuring Scribal Literacy Through Quantitative Analysis
text:
Protosnap’s results


1 2 3 4 5






Protosnap outperformed generic matching methods
The model can generate accurate synthetic cuneiform signs, addressing the lack of labeled data—especially for rare variants
Using synthetic data improved sign classification, especially for rare signs (accuracy: 53.17% vs. 25.84%)




Method is period- and language-agnostic: works for any cuneiform language or era
Next step: quantifying sign and wedge features in a manner interpretable for Assyriologists?

title: Measuring Scribal Literacy Through Quantitative Analysis
text:
What is Geometric-Morphometrics (GMM)?


1 2 3 4 5





GMM quantitatively analyzes shape using geometric coordinates (not just measurements)
Shape is captured by placing landmarks (homologous points) on each object
Variables are the cartesian coordinates of these landmarks
Size is not included; the focus is on shape only
Results can be visualized as images
Several analysis variants exist (e.g., EDMA)

title: Measuring Scribal Literacy Through Quantitative Analysis
text:
GMM Workflow & Procrustes Superimposition


1 2 3 4 5





Collect landmark data (same number & order for all shapes)
Perform Procrustes superimposition to standardize shapes
Analyze shape similarity and difference
Procrustes superimposition:

Removes size, translation, and rotation
Aligns all shapes to a common coordinate system
Also called Procrustes analysis, GPA, or least squares fitting
Enables direct comparison of shape differences

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: Method: a reference space of traditions
text:
Method: a reference space of traditions



Corpus: TLHdig 0.3 XML, 23,526 manuscripts, 1.24 M words, converted following Yavasan and Gordin, From Clay to Code (ALP 2025)
Two feature spaces

word tf-idf (normalised forms) for content
sign n-grams (1–3 signs within a word) for orthography

Traditions as centroids: each tradition is the mean of its manuscripts
Assignment: a fragment goes to its most similar centroid, or to none if the lead over the runner-up is too small (open set)


Reference traditions (StBoT 73, Table 3, plus ritual controls)


Kizzuwatna–Lower Land (Hurrian)
Syro-Mesopotamia (Hurrian), incl. CTH 701
Luwian cult centres
Mixed (Hurrian, Syrian, Luwian)
Kizzuwatna rituals (CTH 471–500)
Old Anatolian rituals (CTH 390–469)


Orphans (CTH 470 + EBo) are never part of the reference.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
text:
Validation: leave one manuscript out


Every manuscript of 17+ words is removed in turn and reassigned. Baselines: always guessing the largest class, and the same procedure with shuffled labels (200 permutations).


Historical groups: 72% over 6 classes, against a 23% majority baseline. CTH 670/701/832 as in the abstract: 89%, but the majority baseline is already 78% (CTH 670 dominates), so it shows little. This is why the reference space moved to historical groups.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: How small can an orphan be?
text:
How small can an orphan be?


Long manuscripts are cut into random windows of k words and reassigned. Words and signs perform alike, and signs are slightly better from about 8 words up.


3 words: about 49%; 10 words: about 60%; 40 words: about 69%, against a chance level of 17%. This curve sets the abstention rule used for the orphans.

Is it vocabulary, orthography, or date?


Remove all logograms (Sumero- and Akkadograms)

word tf-idf: 72% → 66%
sign n-grams: 72% → 70%

The signal survives without the cultic logographic vocabulary.

Script date in CTH 701 (MS vs NS)

the same method cannot predict MS vs NS above the majority baseline

So the 701 groupings are not just script-date clusters.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: Where do CTH 470 and EBo fragments go?
text:
Where do CTH 470 and EBo fragments go?


Orphans with 5+ legible words. A fragment is assigned only when its lead over the runner-up passes the margin at which the coverage experiment reaches 80% precision.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
text:
QTM: orphans as low-coverage witnesses

Each tradition is treated as an archetype, approximated by its most characteristic terms
Each orphan is a witness that attests a small part of it
Coverage asks how much of each archetype the orphans collectively attest
Archetypes with little coverage are transmissions we only see through the reference corpus. High coverage from orphans alone points to traditions that circulated widely in fragments.


E6, first pass: the two ritual traditions (70 and 167 assigned orphans) attest all 200 of their core terms, the Hurrian festival groups 0.64–0.81, and “Mixed” (12 orphans) 0.39. Coverage grows with the number of orphans, so these numbers still need rarefaction (equal orphan counts per tradition) before they can be compared.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
text:
Limits and next steps

Normalisation: TLHdig trans forms are uneven across editors, and broken words are dropped
Preservation bias: short fragments over-represent formulaic lines
Joins: an orphan placed near a known manuscript is a candidate join to check on the tablet
Palaeography: link to sign-shape measurement (DANES 2025) for the same fragments
Philological check: worked examples (top-ranked orphans per tradition) for colleagues to verify
